qtr.text: 2.1.2. Dynamic stress in Harari, as in the other Ethio-Semitic languages, is weakly expressed. Stress has no meaning-distinguishing function and is held not to affect the quantity or quality of vowels. The rules of stress placement in Harari have not been studied systematically. 1151.dq: Any syllable of the Harari noun or verb can be accented, but the accent has no phonemic value in Harari.
1151.dloc: Leslau 1958, The Verb in Harari (South Ethiopic), Introduction p. 4 (last sentence before 'Survey of the verb types'; running header '4 The Verb in Harari')
1151.heavy: a closed word-final syllable (CVC#, with short or long vowel: adáb, basár, dufā́n, buskumā́t, aḥattā́ň) attracts the stress; an open final syllable does not, and stress then goes to the penult (word-final vowels are realized short, §2.1.3, so final CVV does not arise). No role for word-internal weight is stated.
1151.dflt: penultimate (when the final syllable is open: báka, sabára, agáda, diladála, adári, fuṭū́ra)
1151.prule: Weak, non-contrastive dynamic stress with a right-edge coda-weight tendency (Vizirova 2013 §2.1.2, reporting the Introduction to Leslau 1963 Etymological Dictionary of Harari): stress falls on the final syllable when it is closed (adáb, basár, idṓč, dufā́n, birzā́z, buskumā́t, aḥattā́ň, ēlád, dīnát); when the final syllable is open, stress 'as a rule' falls on the penult (báka, sabára, agáda, diladála, adári, ḫā́na, mṓta, ā́ḳa, ā́da, afṓča, gā́yya, dū́da, fuṭū́ra). Stated as a tendency ('тенденция', 'как правило'); placement 'not systematically studied'. Leslau 1958 (accent non-phonemic; type A perfect säbära accented on the 2nd syllable = penult before an open final) and Wagner 1997 (stress not phonemic) are consistent and state no rule of their own.
1151.srule: none described (Vizirova 2013, Leslau 1958 and Wagner 1997 do not mention secondary stress)

tn.quote: The tone-bearing unit in Hausa is the syllable. Hausa has three surface tones. Two are level: Low (L), marked with a grave accent (à and àː); and High (H), left unmarked (a and aː). The third, Falling (F) marked with a circumflex accent (â and âː) is a modulation from the combination of H+L tone on a single syllable. F tones only appear on heavy (CVV and CVC) syllables. Hausa does not have a Rising tone. ... Tone has lexical as well as grammatical functions. ... Tone patterns or melodies are associated with words or morphemes.

Words usually bear a main accent on the penultimate syllable' (o.ku."múná 'to see', o.mu."risè 'herdsman', o."mu.rè 'tall in cl 1', o.ku.hù"ngìrà 'to talk', o.ku.ítá"vèrà 'to agree'), 'Respiratory accents have clearly a word demarcating function'; the main accent shifts to the noun's last syllable before an enclitic demonstrative (o.ka.kà"mbè ngà 'this horse') and to the first syllable in predicative clauses ("lóká.'kàmbè 'it is a horse'). 1156.tone: Elderkin 2003 (the modern primary sketch, standard/southern Herero): two tonal values H and L, every syllable lexically associated with H, L or an HL sequence; utterance-level 'tone keys' (higher/lower pitch registers, Key 1/Key 2), downstep and H-tone spread; the chapter contains no statement of word stress or accent at all. Elderkin adds that northern Herero-related varieties may be influenced by Ndonga/Kwanyama-type systems 'in which high tone seems to have moved to the right and a tonal accent system may be developing', explicitly outside the variety described. Marten & Gibson 2024: lexical + grammatical tone (tone cases, tonal TAM). Möhlig & Kavari 2008 (via Lusekelo 2009): lexical tonal triplet -hórá/-hóra/-hora, extra-high tone. Stress beside tone: Möhlig 2003 sec. 2.2.2 'Respiratory accent' (Google Books view only, page not shown) states 'a primary and a secondary accent can be distinguished. Words usually bear a main accent on the penultimate syllable... Respiratory accents have clearly a word demarcating function', with shifts before enclitic demonstratives and in predicative clauses; the older 'accent' remarks (Kolbe 1883 final ~ penult; Brincker 1886 root syllable; Viehe 1897 root syllable, not fixed, speaker latitude; Meinhof 1909 no rule found) are mutually inconsistent.

1156.cfw: Every modern description agrees that Herero is a tone language with lexical and grammatical high and low tone (Elderkin 2003, Marten and Gibson 2024, Kavari 2025, and the Möhlig and Kavari 2008 grammar as reviewed by Lusekelo 2009), but the one dedicated prosodic study, Möhlig 2003, adds a dynamic main accent that usually falls on the penultimate syllable, and the older grammars disagree with each other on where the accent falls (Brincker 1886 and Viehe 1897 put it on the root syllable, Meinhof 1909 found no rule), so the tonal verdict is secure while the existence and place of word stress beside tone is not.

In practice (Charts V-VI, pp.123, 136-137) verbal aspect and mode are marked entirely by prefixes and infixes (gin-/-in-, m-/n-, -um-, pag-, paga-, pa-, pang-, pakig-, iga-, maka-, ma-), with only the Goal/Referent focus suffixes -on/-an (and hortative -a/-i) at the right edge, while nominal case, number and definiteness are marked by preposed stressless particles (ang/sang/sa, manga): a predominantly prefixing/procliticizing profile with a small set of high-frequency voice suffixes.

vlen.q: Hoava uses five vowels: /i/, /ɛ/, /a/, /ɔ/, /u/. There is no phonemic distinction of vowel length, although vowels can be lengthened when stressed. Kusaghe uses the same set of vowels. The vowels can be combined into pairs with the weight of two syllables.

1164.prule: No phonological stress-placement rule is stated. 1164.cfw: Manoubi (2023), the only full grammar of Hobyot, writes the accent on every form as part of its nominal or verbal scheme and its suffixes and states no placement rule, whereas Simeone-Senelle (2015), a short sketch of the Yemeni variety, gives the Mehri-type rule of stress on the last heavy syllable or else the penult; Manoubi's fuller and more recent description, which finds no phonemic tonic length in Hobyot and treats her long-vowel notation as a Mehri-influenced convention, is the better witness, but the two first-hand accounts disagree about the type of system.

1165.heavy: a syllable whose nucleus is a full (non-schwa) vowel; schwa nuclei cannot bear primary stress; syllable closure plays no role ('no matter whether the word ends in an open syllable... or a closed syllable')

1166.dq: The domain of stress is the metrical foot ... For example, in simple CV.CV words, the first syllable is always more prominent. ... The phonological foot in Ho (the domain of stress and harmony) is not equal to the grammatical word.

1166.heavy: Heavy syllables include CVV (long vowels and diphthongs) and CVC. Superheavy syllables (CVVC) do not behave differently from heavy syllables for stress assignment. Light = CV or VC; extra-light = V (extrametrical).
1166.prule: Predictable, trochaic word stress counted from the left: in CV.CV words the first syllable is stressed; if the second syllable is heavier than the first (heavy = CVV or CVC; CVVC behaves as heavy; light = CV/VC), stress falls on the second syllable instead. Onsetless V-only syllables are extra-light and extrametrical (never stressed, skipped in the count), so V-initial words stress the following syllable (or the one after it if heavier).
1166.srule: Tentative (author: 'it seems'): in four-syllable words a second, weaker stress falls in the second foot of the word, treated as secondary stress, e.g. [me.ˈtai.ˌte.na], [ca.ˈbaː.ˌka.na], [a.ˈyu.mi.la.ˌgiã] (initial V extrametrical); placement judged impressionistically (fn. 2); nothing stated for longer words.

qtr.text: VII.A. STRESS. In most words of two or more syllables the stress is on the penultimate syllable. The exceptions are words that end in certain syllables, such as (-ta), (-ⁿda) or (-na), (ne), (-a), et al. ['at al.' sic], in which the stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable. In isolated elicited responses with the above suffixes some variation in stress placement has been observed. In verbs with a series of suffixes, the placement of stress and of vowel length is more complex; it may turn out that the suffixes are clitics.

In virtually any sort of text, slightly more than half of the morphemes which occur are suffixes.' The verbal word is root/stem + (pre-transition suffixes) + transition (object-tense-subject suffixes) + (post-transition suffixes) (§7.1 p.75, §8.1.2 p.92); the substantive is root + possessive + plural + case + shading + evidential + post-positions (Table 7-4, §7.2.2.1 p.83).

Clause-final words (and all words in isolation): main stress on the non-final heavy syllable; if no non-final heavy syllable, on the INITIAL syllable. Clause-internal words: normally initial stress (slow speech: tendency to stress a non-initial heavy syllable, esp. the last non-final one). Stress is 'in the process of shifting to the initial syllable'. Examples: [sipásta.] clause-final vs [sípasta] clause-internal; [wayínco], [munámpaq], [kánaq], [súmaq], [úk]. In clause-final CVCVCV words intensity is initial but pitch slightly higher on the penult (intonation). Rest of Ancash (outside huay1240): penultimate stress.

The final-syllable cases (interjections, a small class of noun roots with a stressed final syllable, a word-final long syllable esp. 1sg /-: as in [peqá:], [mikú:]) are placements of the primary stress and are listed under exceptions; borrowed conjunctions /i/, /o/ (sometimes /huk/, /kay/, /cay/) are unstressed; Spanish loans follow the native patterns.
